title: Ford’s new electric truck, ‘Fathom,’ starts at $28,350
teaser: Ford's next-gen electric truck, Fathom, starts near $30k, aiming to leapfrog competitors and solidify Ford's EV future.
summary: Ford is positioning its next-generation all-electric pickup, the Fathom, as a crucial new venture built on its 'Universal EV Platform.' Set for preorders in early 2027 and delivery in fall 2027, the vehicle is designed to be Ford's second electric truck after the F-150 Lightning. Starting at $28,350 (or $29,945 with fees), it includes features like Apple Maps integration and support for Android Auto/Apple CarPlay. The Fathom will also feature BlueCruise capability and potentially offer supervised driving by 2028. While Ford hopes the vehicle can counter rising competition from Chinese EVs, its success hinges on navigating a tricky market where most buyers still prefer SUVs over compact pickups.
author: Sean O'Kane
content: Ford's next-generation electric truck will be called Fathom, and it will start at $28,350 when it goes on sale in 2027, the company said on Thursday. A "destination and delivery" fee will bring that price up to $29,945, putting the Fathom just below the $30,000 mark that Ford has targeted since it first started talking more openly about the project in 2025. The truck, when it arrives next year, represents a major bet for Ford. It's the automaker's second all-electric truck after the F-150 Lightning (third, if you count the limited-run Ranger EV from the late 1990s). But like many of its peers, the company has dramatically pulled back on its once-ambitious plans to build electric vehicles. The Fathom is the first vehicle Ford is building on its new "Universal EV Platform," or UEV, which will power a number of different EVs and involves a brand-new assembly line process meant to cut costs. It's an attempt by CEO Jim Farley to try and catch up to category leader Tesla, as well as the many Chinese EVs that he's argued against allowing into the U.S. market - all while building the truck in Louisville, Kentucky. Deliveries begin in "fall 2027," and Ford said on Thursday that it won't reveal the truck until "early 2027," which is when it will start taking preorders. We do have some details, though. Ford has already said the Fathom will have Apple Maps built into its operating system, and on Thursday, the company said the truck will support Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. Notably, it will not support Apple's next-generation CarPlay Ultra. The Fathom will have five seats, which is more interior space than a Toyota RAV4; a "large, high-resolution touch screen," and a "digital car key." It will be capable of bidirectional power, much like the Lightning and the hybrid F-150. Every Fathom will also be "BlueCruise-capable," meaning it will come with the tech integrated, but buyers will likely have to pay extra to enable Ford's hands-free advanced driver assistance system. The truck is supposed to have a newer, more powerful version of BlueCruise that Ford says will eventually be capable of handling supervised driving from starting point to destination. Eyes-off driving is expected in 2028. The Fathom's starting price also only includes the "standard range" lithium iron phosphate battery pack. Ford hasn't yet said how many miles the truck can drive on a single charge. Ford said the name represents "a deep understanding of the person who would drive" the truck, and how their "motivations look a little different from the traditional truck customer's." "[T]he name had to do more than sound good. It had to capture a mindset, shifting the focus from specs to a spirit of adaptability," the company wrote. Electric trucks have not done terribly well in the U.S. The Lightning only moved a little more than 10,000 units in its best quarter , and though Tesla's Cybertruck had a higher peak, it has since crashed out. Ford is gambling by choosing the truck form factor for its first UEV platform vehicle. But there are some inherent upsides: The Fathom and other vehicles built on the platform will be the first that Ford has designed from the ground up to use electric powertrains. That should mean fewer tradeoffs on range, efficiency, and overall packaging of the vehicle. Both the Fathom and UEV have been in the works for a few years. It started as a skunkworks project that Farley tasked former Tesla exec Alan Clarke with leading, as TechCrunch first reported in 2024 . The team is flush with talent from Rivian, Tesla, and Apple's now-defunct car project, and has purportedly been working in isolation in Los Angeles, separated from the bureaucracy of the rest of the company. All of this likely contributed to getting the Fathom's starting price to just under $30,000, a major accomplishment in a market where the average new car costs $50,000. The truck won't have a lot of competition in that range - it's essentially going up against just the spartan, Jeff Bezos-backed Slate pickup, and a few non-truck EVs like the Chevy Bolt. Ford has found a ton of success with its small, low-cost Maverick pickup, which comes in both internal combustion and hybrid powertrain variants. The Fathom is an attempt to bottle that lightning, without going the way of the Lightning.

title: Amid legal battles, Suno says it will start watermarking songs
teaser: Amid major lawsuits, Suno will implement watermarking and stringent policies to fight misuse of its AI-generated music.
summary: Suno, the AI song creation service, is implementing significant changes—including audio watermarking, fingerprinting, and updated download policies—to combat misuse of its tracks amidst multiple legal battles. Co-founder Mikey Shulman emphasized that these tools aim for transparency without judging art quality. Key updates include signing an agreement with Musixmatch for copyright detection and changing community guidelines to explicitly prohibit 'deceptive audio presented as real' or unauthorized use of a person’s voice/likeness. The company, which recently raised $400 million in Series D funding, is facing lawsuits from UMG and Sony Music Group, and a German court previously ruled it violated copyright rules (GEMA). Furthermore, Suno was linked to a November 2025 data breach affecting an alleged 55 million users.
author: Ivan Mehta
content: Suno, the service that allows users to create AI-generated songs, today announced new tools to mark tracks made on its platform, limit downloads, and update community guidelines to prevent copycat songs. The changes come as Suno faces numerous lawsuits from labels and artist bodies . In a blog post , co-founder and CEO Mikey Shulman shared core principles and said that the platform wants to promote original creation while enabling more people to make music with its AI tools. One of the key points of contention involved users uploading AI-generated songs on other streaming platforms and gaming the system to earn revenue. Suno said that now it will use audio watermarking and fingerprinting to prevent misuse on other streaming platforms. It's not clear if Suno will use an existing system like Google's Synth ID or adopt a new one, and the company did not say when contacted by TechCrunch about this. The startup also signed an agreement with lyrics provider Musixmatch to use its Sentinel system for copyright detection, the blog post said. "These tools are designed to be durable and resistant to tampering, without affecting the listening experience. They are also not intended to pass judgment on whether a song is good, meaningful, or sufficiently human," said Shulman in the blog. "Ultimately, we believe it should be up to artists and platforms to decide what they want to disclose. Our role is to build tools that give them transparency options and make it easier to collaborate across the industry." The company added that it plans to add a new download policy to bar mass distribution on streaming platforms, but declined to provide details on the record. Suno has also changed its community guidelines to explicitly prohibit "deceptive audio presented as real" and "using a real person's voice or likeness without permission" to prevent copycats. The company, which raised $400 million in a Series D funding round in June , is fighting legal battles on many fronts. The startup is in a lawsuit with the Universal Music Group (UMG) and Sony Music Group in a case coordinated by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). Late last month, a German court ruled in favor of a government-mandated licensing agency, GEMA, and said Suno was breaking copyright rules . Separately, 404 Media reported that Suno experienced a data breach in November 2025, which revealed that the platform scraped YouTube, Deezer, and Genius to train its models. Later, data breach notification service Have I Been Pwned said that the data breach affected 55 million users . The startup now faces a class action lawsuit in Massachusetts, which alleges that the company overlooked security measures to focus on profit .

title: Snowflake extortionist admits 165-victim cloud crime spree – and squeezing one target twice
teaser: Snowflake extortionist Connor Moucka pleads guilty after compromising 165+ organizations and pocketing $495,000 from a multi-million dollar cloud crime spree.
summary: A Canadian cybercriminal, Connor Moucka (26), has pleaded guilty to orchestrating a massive data theft campaign targeting cloud customers linked to Snowflake. He admitted that he and co-conspirators exploited stolen credentials to breach over 165 organizations between February and October 2024, compromising billions of records. The stolen data included highly sensitive information like Social Security numbers, banking details, driver's licenses, and payroll records. Moucka confessed to developing software to search compromised cloud environments for valuable targets, demanding millions in ransoms (about $2.5 million received), and even re-extorting a victim who had already paid a ransom in May 2024. Victims suffered over $9.5 million in direct losses, not including the harm to an estimated 100 million individuals whose personal data was compromised.
content: storage Snowflake extortionist admits 165-victim cloud crime spree - and squeezing one target twice Connor Moucka pleads guilty over sprawling 2024 campaign that looted billions of records A Canadian who helped orchestrate the sprawling Snowflake-linked data theft campaign has pleaded guilty in the US, admitting that he and his co-conspirators returned to squeeze at least one victim a second time. Connor Riley Moucka, 26, of Kitchener, Ontario, admitted computer fraud, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft, and conspiracy charges over a hacking spree that compromised more than 165 organizations, exposed billions of customer records, and brought in about $2.5 million in ransom payments. According to the US Department of Justice , Moucka and his co-conspirators used stolen login credentials to break into the cloud environments of at least 165 customers of a US software provider between February and October 2024. The DOJ still doesn't name the company, but the allegations match the 2024 campaign against Snowflake customers that ensnared the likes of Ticketmaster, Santander, AT&T , and dozens of others. In a plea agreement seen by The Register , Moucka admitted developing software that automatically searched compromised cloud environments for valuable information. He and his co-conspirators used it to identify lucrative targets and steal terabytes of banking records, payroll data, passport and driver's license numbers, Social Security numbers, DEA registration numbers, and other sensitive information. They then threatened to publish the haul unless victims paid up. Moucka also admitted that the conspirators returned to at least one victim after it paid a ransom in May 2024, demanding more money months later to prevent the stolen customer data from being published or sold. The second attempt used stolen records concerning a government official and members of a former government official's immediate family. The stolen data was also advertised for sale on cybercrime forums including BreachForums, Exploit.in, and XSS.is, as well as via Telegram, according to prosecutors. The group demanded at least $6 million from its victims and received about 36 Bitcoin, then worth roughly $2.5 million. Moucka admitted pocketing at least $495,000. Victim organizations suffered more than $9.5 million in direct losses, though the DOJ said that figure does not include downstream harm affecting at least 100 million individuals whose personal information was exposed. Moucka was arrested in Canada in October 2024 , just months after investigators linked him to the attacks, and was extradited to the US in July this year. He is due to be sentenced on October 27. Aggravated identity theft carries a mandatory two-year prison term that must run consecutively to any other sentence, while the other offences carry varying maximum penalties. A federal judge will determine Moucka's sentence. ®

title: OPSWAT targets file regeneration over detection for critical infrastructure security
teaser: Traditional cybersecurity defenses are dangerously slow against AI-powered attacks; experts argue that prevention via file regeneration is the only viable fix for critical infrastructure.
summary: Critical infrastructure security must evolve beyond detection. Benny Czarny of OPSWAT argues that AI-powered attacks are too fast for traditional detect-and-respond models, especially where downtime is impossible (e.g., power grids or nuclear facilities). Instead, he advocates for prevention through file regeneration using Deep Content Disarm and Reconstruction (CDR) technology. This method assumes all files are potentially malicious, parsing them to create a clean version that is mathematically free of embedded threats. Beyond software, peripheral media (like USB drives and charging cables) pose underestimated risks; thus, security requires monitoring *all* data flow—downloads, uploads, emails, and external devices. Implementing this 'firewall of data' significantly boosts resilience.
author: Thomas Godwin
content: Critical infrastructure security faces a novel threat of the sort that detection-based defenses were never designed to handle, and the critical personnel who run our power grids, water plants and financial systems can't afford to learn this the hard way. Benny Czarny (pictured), CEO and founder of OPSWAT Inc., makes this argument clear in his USA Today bestselling book, Cybersecurity Upside Down . Czarny said AI has dramatically accelerated the speed and targeting precision of file-borne attacks, making the traditional detect-and-respond model all but obsolete. Response models are dangerously slow in an environment where 99% uptime is not good enough and taking systems offline for investigation or patching is often impossible. "Whenever we look at critical infrastructure and how to protect it, the network is extremely complex, and you can't really afford to have any downtime," Czarny said. "Think about it. You run a nuclear facility, or you run defense, or you are running a very important financial service. 99% is not enough." Czarny spoke with Krista Case at Black Hat USA during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed why prevention through file regeneration is more effective than detection for critical infrastructure security, how peripheral media remains a dangerously underestimated attack vector and what OPSWAT's bootstrapped growth model has meant for its product focus and customer relationships. (* Disclosure below.) Critical infrastructure security demands prevention through file regeneration OPSWAT's Deep Content Disarm and Reconstruction technology takes a radically disparate approach to critical infrastructure security. Instead of identifying malicious files, Deep CDR assumes all incoming files are potentially compromised, parses their structure and regenerates a clean version that's mathematically free of embedded threats. The process is deterministic, meaning it doesn't rely on signature databases or behavioral heuristics that AI-powered attacks can increasingly evade. "You achieve prevention through file regeneration, not through detection," Czarny said. "You assume that all of the file flow to your organization is malicious, and then you regenerate a new file that is malware-free." Peripheral media represents one of the most underestimated attack surfaces in OT environments. The threats go well beyond USB drives, including SD cards, phones, contractor laptops, external drives and even charging cables, Czarny noted. Device-based threats consist of hardware that masquerades as peripheral media while functioning as a network sniffer or a remote access tool. USB kill devices can deliver up to 240 volts of electrical power to a programmable logic controller, physically destroying equipment and shutting down a facility. Mapping and intercepting every data channel (file downloads, uploads, email attachments and peripheral media simultaneously) is the foundation of what Czarny refers to as a firewall of data. "Think about intercepting all of your data flow from file downloads, file upload, USBs, external peripheral media, email attachments," Czarny said. "If you do that, you can eliminate so many threats and increase your cybersecurity posture and resilience significantly." For practitioners looking to start, Czarny recommended OPSWAT Academy as the most direct path to building the foundational skills necessary to implement a preventative architecture. The program has certified nearly 289,000 professionals to date. "We make cybersecurity fun and exciting and visual to a point that anybody can understand," Czarny said. "Episode one is about breaking the firewall - we're mythbusting that the firewall is effective." title: eBay continues to bet on live shopping after record quarter
teaser: eBay Live's GMV jumped eightfold year-over-year, proving that live shopping is becoming an essential revenue stream across global e-commerce.
summary: Despite facing stiff competition from platforms like TikTok Shop and Whatnot, resale giant eBay is accelerating its commitment to live shopping via 'eBay Live.' Following a quarter of record performance, the platform reported that its GMV jumped roughly eightfold year-over-year across seven global markets. The success metrics are highly encouraging: over 90% of regular streamers saw growth, and users who leverage Live sell about three times more than non-Live participants. Furthermore, first-time collectibles shoppers spent nearly 70% more. eBay is now making the service self-service for hundreds of categories and expanding globally, solidifying live commerce as a major growth engine beyond a mere trend.
author: Lauren Forristal
content: As eBay tries to keep up with competitors like Whatnot and TikTok Shop, the online marketplace is making a bigger push into live shopping after seeing record results. During its second-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, the company noted that eBay Live's gross merchandise volume (GMV) jumped about eight times year-over-year across seven markets, along with increases in viewers, watch time, and items sold. It plans to expand eBay Live to more international markets in the coming weeks and months. "These results reinforce our confidence that Live can deepen engagement, broaden discovery, and increase velocity across the broader eBay marketplace," CEO Jamie Iannone told investors. However, it's important to note that eBay didn't share the exact GMV number, making it difficult to assess how significant the growth is. That said, eBay clearly sees Live as a key growth area, and the feedback from sellers and buyers looks promising. eBay reports that over 90% of sellers who stream regularly have seen their GMV grow, and those who use Live sell about three times more than those who don't. Buyers are also spending more. First-time shoppers in the collectibles category are dropping around 70% more than their non-Live shopping counterparts. eBay launched Live as invite-only in the U.S. in 2022, then expanded internationally, starting with a beta in the U.K. in 2024, and it has since rolled it out in countries like Germany, Australia, France, Italy, and Canada. Last month, the company moved past its invite-only model and now offers self-service onboarding for eligible sellers in over 300 categories, which include everything from electronics to fashion and collectibles. The company also pointed to recent product improvements, including discovery features across its homepage and mobile app to make live events easier to find. Iannone added that eBay also simplified event creation, inventory preparation, and live item management for sellers, while improving "bidding responsiveness" to create smoother, faster livestreams. The growth comes as live shopping in the U.S. moves beyond a niche trend, with more companies beginning to treat it more seriously rather than a side experiment. Even resale giant StockX recently introduced live shopping capabilities. Whatnot continues to find success, with a valuation of more than $11 billion. Additionally, TikTok Shop is reportedly testing a paid membership that offers free shipping and exclusive discounts.

title: Microsoft excludes Domain Exclusion from MS 365 Copilot  – days after rolling it out
teaser: Microsoft abruptly withdrew Copilot’s Domain Exclusion feature after promising it was key for web-grounding. Experts say a blocklist is backwards; they demand an approved allow list.
summary: Microsoft has suddenly withdrawn 'Domain Exclusion' for MS 365 Copilot, a feature designed to manage the AI assistant’s reliance on web data. Originally, Domain Exclusion allowed administrators to create a blacklist of up to 1,000 untrusted web domains, helping ensure Copilot answers aligned with organizational policies and trusted sources. However, Microsoft rolled back the control without providing a reason, stating they are 'actively evaluating next steps.' Critics argue that managing an ever-growing list of prohibited sites (a 'block list') is difficult and cumbersome. Instead, experts suggest adopting an 'allow list' model, which would restrict Copilot only to pre-approved domains, offering better governance.
content: AI AND ML Microsoft excludes Domain Exclusion from MS 365 Copilot - days after rolling it out Perhaps an allow list of domains might be better? Microsoft has abruptly withdrawn Domain Exclusion for Microsoft 365 Copilot, days after touting it as a way to stop the assistant grounding its answers in unwanted websites. If you had a list of sources you didn't trust, you're out of luck for now. Microsoft announced Domain Exclusion last month. The idea was simple and sensible: Copilot can consult the public web when answering questions, but that also gives it ample opportunity to suck in nonsense. Administrators were to be given some control over the sources it used. Health warnings about AI output only go so far when Microsoft wants businesses to put Copilot into critical workflows. As the company put it, "admins need practical controls that help web-grounded experiences stay aligned with organizational policies, compliance expectations, and trusted source strategies." Enter Domain Exclusion, which was designed to let organizations bar up to 1,000 web domains from influencing Copilot responses. Administrators could create the list from a CSV file using PowerShell. Microsoft stated: "By helping admins reduce the influence of unwanted or non-compliant web sources, Domain Exclusion supports a more governed approach to AI adoption." Except it no longer does. In an update this week, Microsoft said the feature "has been rolled back at this time." The company did not give a reason for the abrupt rollback, only stating: "We understand the importance of this capability and are actively evaluating next steps." The control was welcome, but its block list design promised administrators an endless game of Whac-A-Mole. A ceiling of 1,000 domains looks modest beside the size of the public web, and staff could potentially use Copilot to retrieve information from sites that organizational policies barred them from visiting directly. An allow list of approved sources would turn that burden around, limiting Copilot to sites the organization already trusts. At the time of Microsoft's announcement, one commenter remarked: "I really wish this was the other way around: Off, but add an allow list. The On, but disable some means we'd have to know which sites were 'bad.' Seems backwards to do it that way." ®

title: Gen Z dating apps like Ditto ditch swiping in favor of AI matchmaking
teaser: The swipe era is ending: New apps like Ditto are ditching swipes entirely, using AI matchmaking and mandatory group dates to reconnect disillusioned Gen Z users.
summary:
Driven by Gen Z's dissatisfaction with endless swiping on apps like Tinder and Hinge, the dating industry is undergoing a major shift toward real-world connection. New platforms and established players are abandoning swipe mechanics for group meetups and advanced AI matchmaking.
Ditto, co-founded by Allen Wang and Eric Liu, exemplifies this trend. Instead of traditional swiping, users interact with an AI chatbot that uses sophisticated algorithms to predict chemistry based on personality signals derived from interests. The platform mandates structured dates every week, removing friction for its 150,000 signups.
Major competitors like Bumble are also responding; they launched 'Plans' for low-pressure group settings and their CEO confirmed the decline of the swipe era. Both companies recognize that group socializing is now the preferred method for Gen Z to meet people, marking a fundamental change in consumer expectations for online dating.
author: Amanda Silberling
content: This generation of twentysomethings is so disillusioned with swipe-based dating apps that they'll try literally anything else - even an AI matchmaker. After dropping out of UC Berkeley, Ditto co-founders Allen Wang and Eric Liu set out to build something that would help their peers connect without having to spend hours each week navigating the messiness of apps like Tinder and Hinge. "As Gen Z ourselves, we were firsthand witnessing the behavioral shift in terms of how people are connecting with each other," Wang told TechCrunch. "We see that people are getting super tired of all the endless swiping and endless small talk, and they're really looking for something more genuine in real life." Instead of a typical app, college students can sign up for Ditto by texting a certain iMessage number, along with a code. Then an AI chatbot introduces itself as Ditto, "a dating initiative built by college students who get it ... no swiping, no awkward DMs, just real dates every Wednesday at 7 pm." Image Credits: Ditto (opens in a new window) Users text their way through an onboarding process, starting with basic biographical information like their name, gender, and birth date. Then Ditto gets into more specific questions to understand someone's personality, interests, and dating preferences. Some users even upload photos of their celebrity crushes to give the AI a sense of their type. The Ditto algorithm tries to match people not based on similar hobbies and interests, but rather what those hobbies and interests say about who someone is. "If there's this guy, and he's really into rock climbing, skydiving, and outdoor sports, and this girl, if she's into hip hop, streetwear, and skateboarding, then even though those hobbies don't look similar on the surface, I can tell you deeper down, both are very adventurous; maybe they're very individualistic," Wang said. "So that's actually the core reason why people will find chemistry with each other, and so basically our claim is that chemistry is actually predictable with the right signals." Then, every Wednesday at 7 p.m., Ditto messages users with their match for the week. "It comes with the person, it comes with a time, it comes with a location, and the users simply just need to show up and date each other and come back. We'll collect more feedback about the date, and then improve our understanding of the user, and send them to a better next date," Wang said. "Right now people's goal is really just to go out there and meet each other, so it's actually removing a lot of friction for our users, so that we are doing the heavy lifting for them, and they just simply go there and then meet whoever." Image Credits: Ditto (opens in a new window) Ditto has 150,000 signups, and Wang says that out of all the matches that are connected via Ditto, about 20% of those matches end up going out on a date. (If that percentage sounds low to you, then you've probably never used Tinder.) Ditto creates a collage-like graphic to introduce users to one another and explain why they might be a good match - it's a popular aesthetic among Gen Z that other connection apps with young founders like Sonder have gravitated toward. With any dating app, and especially one that minimizes the time between matching and going out, it can be hard to discern the safety of a situation - is the person you're meeting really who they say they are? For now, while Ditto is only available at a few dozen colleges, there's a built-in vetting process in which you know that someone is a student at your university with a .edu email. Ditto is focused on figuring out how to grow to more schools - and eventually beyond just college - while scaling safely. Even for the most established and well-funded dating apps, this is a challenging endeavor. But Ditto does have $9.2 million in seed funding to work with from investors like Gradient, Peak XV, and Scribble. Wang said, "99% of the investors just reached out to us through inbound, because we were pretty big on LinkedIn and Twitter for a bit. Even Duolingo's co-founder Severin [Hacker] reached out to me saying, 'Hey, love your mission, I really like what you do, let's hop on a call.'" Ditto has been able to establish this notoriety through its irreverent marketing, like videos of robot stunts . Now based in San Francisco, Ditto has 12 full-time employees, but they're also hiring a " chief yacht officer " to throw promotional parties (yes, this is a legitimate job listing). "Our users are college students, and they can smell corporate marketing from a mile away," Wang said. "But the stunts are the top of the funnel, not the product ... Viral moments get college kids to look; a good first date is what makes them stay."

title: Google Wallet now lets parents set up secure balances for their kids
teaser: Parents can now set up secure digital balances in Google Wallet, giving them unprecedented control over their kids' spending and finances.
summary: Google has launched a major feature within Google Wallet, enabling parents to create secure digital spending balances for their children under 18. This system is designed to foster financial literacy while giving parents comprehensive control. Parents can establish daily spending limits, monitor all transaction history, and receive real-time notifications of purchases. Key safeguards include the ability to lock or unlock the account remotely and activate a temporary 'spending timeout.' Kids can use their Android or Wear OS devices for tap-to-pay payments where Google Pay is accepted, helping them learn money management without requiring a traditional bank account. This competitive move places Google Wallet alongside tools like Apple Cash Family.
author: Aisha Malik
content: Google announced on Thursday that Google Wallet will now allow parents to set up a secure balance for children under 18. The tech giant says the new feature is designed to help parents teach healthy financial habits while maintaining oversight of their child's spending through built-in safeguards. Parents can set daily spending limits, review their child's transaction history, and choose to receive notifications whenever a purchase is made. Parents can also lock or unlock the account if the child's device is lost, or activate a temporary "spending timeout" to pause spending at any time. The new feature brings Google Wallet more in line with competing financial tools, including Apple Cash Family, which lets parents send money to their children while monitoring transactions and managing spending controls. Additionally, the company is positioning itself against startups like FamZoo and Greenlight , which allow parents to teach their children financial literacy through prepaid debit card systems. Image Credits: Google / Kids can use their Android device or Wear OS devices to tap and pay wherever Google Pay is accepted. The tech giant sees the new feature as a way for kids to manage their own money without the need for an actual bank account. The update is rolling out in the United States. It's unknown when, or if, Google plans to bring the new capability to additional regions. The new feature builds on Google's announcement last year that parents and guardians in select countries can allow their children to use digital payments on Android devices under parental supervision. A payment card can only be added with parental consent, and parents receive an email whenever their child makes a transaction. With last year's update, kids also gained the ability to use Google Wallet to access supported passes, like event tickets, library cards, and gift cards.

title: ChatGPT brings unlimited text chats to free users
teaser: Great news for free ChatGPT users: OpenAI is removing text chat limits and upgrading the default AI model.
summary: OpenAI is rolling out significant updates across all ChatGPT user tiers. For free and Go users, text chat limits are being removed, and the default AI model is upgraded to GPT-5.6 Luna, while they gain a new 'Think' button for complex queries. Paid subscribers (Plus/Pro) receive an enhanced GPT-5.6 Sol model, designed to provide more reliable, fact-checked responses with tighter formatting. This updated version, along with a new thinking slider that lets users adjust the model's complexity, was noted to reduce factual errors by up to 68% compared to previous versions.
author: Ivan Mehta
content: OpenAI is removing limits on text-based chats for all users on ChatGPT, which recently crossed the 1 billion weekly user mark , the company announced today. The new GPT-5.6 Luna model will power this experience and will be the default model for Free and Go users, replacing GPT-5.5. Both users will also get a new "Think" button that lets them select higher reasoning power for complex questions. OpenAI said that there will still be separate limits for files, images, voice, and image generation. Image Credits: OpenAI The update brings changes for Plus and Pro users as well. They'll gain access to an upgraded GPT-5.6 Sol model that's better for quick tasks such as questions, web research, advice, planning, writing, and making decisions. The company noted that this new model will give more compact and robust answers. (Notably, this is a separate version from GPT-5.6 Sol used for Codex and Work, which is unchanged.) ChatGPT Plus and Pro users are also getting a thinking slider to adjust "how much" thought the model puts into an answer. They can tune the thinking slider based on complexity and steps involved in solving a query. Image Credits: OpenAI OpenAI said an internal evaluation found that, compared to GPT-5.5-Instant, factual errors were 62% less common for GPT-5.6 Luna and 68% less common for GPT-5.6 Sol. The updated version of GPT-5.6 Sol is available to Plus and Pro users today, while the other changes for Free and Go users are arriving this week. Next week, users will gain access to unlimited text chats and the new Think button for harder questions.

title: CISOs face a defining test as AI reshapes where enterprise risk decisions get made
teaser: CISOs' role is shifting: they must guide corporate decision-makers on accepting massive AI risks, rather than just blocking attacks.
summary: AI-driven cyberattacks are fundamentally changing the role of the CISO, forcing them beyond traditional defense strategies and into high-level enterprise decision-making. The CISO must now function as the 'connective tissue' across business units like legal and compliance, guiding discussions on acceptable corporate risk levels. Experts note that a significant gap exists in preparedness: only about 20% of CISOs have formed a coherent AI strategy. To succeed, security leaders must shift focus from simply blocking threats to building threat models linked to specific business initiatives, empowering executives with clear choices: whether to accept, mitigate, or transfer the associated risk.
author: Kelly Knight
content: CISO AI risk management is emerging as the defining test of the AI era, pushing security leaders beyond blocking attacks and into the middle of enterprise decisions about how much risk a business is willing to accept. That tension is playing out this week as thousands of practitioners converge on Las Vegas, where AI has propelled the cybersecurity world into a new phase, driven by startlingly advanced autonomous attacks and an urgent need to adopt technology to defend against them. Much of that pressure is now landing squarely on the CISO, who is increasingly expected to act as connective tissue across legal, compliance, engineering and the business itself, according to Krista Case (pictured, left), principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research. "I've also been thinking about this AI governance through the lens of the different roles that the CISO has to collaborate with within the enterprise - things like legal, compliance, engineering, IT," Case said. "They almost have to be sort of the connective tissue helping to facilitate these conversations. So they're really becoming a business enabler." Case was joined by Jon Oltsik (right), analyst in residence at theCUBE Research, for a keynote analysis of Black Hat USA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed how the CISO role is evolving as AI moves from experimentation into production , alongside the invite-only summits where senior cybersecurity executives participate in candid, confidential conversation that will help to shape the next generation of cybersecurity strategy. ( * Disclosure below.) CISO AI risk management splits the market into leaders and laggards That evolution remains far from universal. Only a narrow slice of security leaders have translated AI hype into a coherent strategy, Oltsik said. "About 20% of CISOs get it," he said. "They understand the implications, they understand what their organization's trying to do with AI. ... They're looking at security architecturally. ... The other 80% are in a state of ignorance, sometimes ignorance is bliss, or at least assumed bliss." That gap in AI risk management is compounded by a disconnect between the tools flooding the show floor and the practitioners meant to evaluate them, according to Oltsik. Instead, CISOs must build threat models tied to specific business initiatives, then hand executives a clear menu of choices - accept, mitigate or transfer the risk - rather than stand in the way of adoption, he said. "You can't get in the way, and no one should try to get in the way - you'll get run over," Oltsik said. "You'll lose your job if you try to get in the way. So that's really the way it is." title: Blue Origin blames New Glenn fireball on engine oxygen valve
teaser: Blue Origin blames a faulty oxygen valve on a key component, identifying it as the cause of New Glenn's recent fiery explosion.
summary: Blue Origin has pinpointed the main cause of the May New Glenn rocket explosion: an anomaly originating at the primary oxygen valve on one BE-4 engine. During a preflight hotfire test at Cape Canaveral, the failure led to the destruction of the rocket and equipment. CEO Dave Limp confirmed this diagnosis, noting that the company is rapidly modifying and retrofitting updated valves to existing engines. While the original goal was to launch in 2026, Blue Origin is restructuring its assembly process. The BE-4 engine also powers United Launch Alliance's Vulcan, which operates independently from this anomaly.
content: SCIENCE Blue Origin blames New Glenn fireball on engine oxygen valve Small modifications under way as Bezos's rocket biz races to rebuild pad and fly again this year Blue Origin has identified the engine component at the center of May's spectacular New Glenn pad explosion, which left the Jeff Bezos space tentacle facing a substantial rebuild. "The anomaly originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines, which was later confirmed by hardware recovery and inspections," CEO Dave Limp posted . Limp did not explain the valve's failure mode or explain how the anomaly led to the explosion. New Glenn, whose first stage is powered by seven BE-4 engines, was on the pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station's Launch Complex 36 for a preflight hotfire test in May when it suddenly exploded . The blast destroyed the rocket and key ground equipment. Blue Origin has since been rebuilding the facility at a breakneck pace. In June, Limp said the company still planned to launch in 2026 and later explained that the replacement pad would support a revised integration process. The stages will be assembled horizontally and rolled out before the payload is mated with New Glenn in the vertical position. Limp said extensive component-level and engine hotfire tests had been conducted "to understand the failure mode better and inform mitigations." "The path forward is clear," he wrote. "We're making small modifications to the valve that can be quickly retrofitted to existing engines. We're manufacturing the updated hardware, which will be ready by the end of this month." Blue Origin is not the only BE-4 customer. United Launch Alliance (ULA) uses two of the engines on Vulcan's first stage. Vulcan is already sidelined from US Space Force missions following an unrelated anomaly in a Northrop Grumman solid rocket booster during its last launch in February. The payload reached orbit, but the Space Force wants the problem resolved before Vulcan flies for it again. ULA did not immediately respond when asked whether its stock of BE-4 engines would require the same valve modifications. ®

title: TikTok lays off 250 employees, shutters its Nashville office

Despite the cuts, the company reiterated its commitment to maintaining a 'secure, safe and positive experience' for its 200 million American users. author: Aisha Malik
content: TikTok is laying off 250 employees and closing its Nashville office, which housed some members of TikTok's content-moderation team. The news was first reported by The New York Times . The Nashville office, which TikTok leased in 2024, will close on October 5.

title: Azure CTO pastes Doom into Paint one frame at a time
teaser: Azure CTO Mark Russinovich turned MS Paint into a display monitor for Doom by piping every frame through the Windows clipboard.
summary: Azure CTO Mark Russinovich launched a whimsical technical demonstration by turning Microsoft Paint into a display screen for the classic game Doom. The unorthodox setup streams every frame of Doom (rendered by ViZDoom) directly onto Paint's canvas using the Windows clipboard as its transfer mechanism. Russinovich, acknowledging it was 'frivolous,' showcased that technology can be used for fun experiments. He also noted leveraging AI tools like Claude and Fable 5 in his development process.
content: OFFBEAT Azure CTO pastes Doom into Paint one frame at a time It computes nothing, renders everything, and even has sound Microsoft Azure CTO Mark Russinovich has taken a break from the cloud to turn Paint into a monitor for Doom, using the Windows clipboard as plumbing. Dubbed "MS Paint Doom" or "DoomPaint" - either will work - the project is the product of a spare-time experiment. To be clear, Microsoft Paint isn't doing anything other than serving as a place to paste from the game. As Russinovich observed: "Paint renders the game but does not compute it. Paint computes nothing. Paint has never computed anything. That's the joke." The result is as enjoyable as it is pointless. Doom still runs in the background and, on the PC we tried, the framerate was hardly fluid. The important thing was that it worked. There was even sound. ViZDoom runs the Doom .wad file and renders it headlessly. Each frame is passed through the Windows clipboard and pasted onto Paint's canvas. A low-level keyboard hook captures and swallows game inputs while Paint is in the foreground, and sound effects come from the game engine. A glance at the code shows Russinovich was more than happy to use Claude to whip it up. In a LinkedIn post , he said: "I've been using Fable 5 on serious research projects and find it a noticeable improvement over Opus 4.8." Using Microsoft Paint as a display for Doom is not, however, a serious research project, as Russinovich acknowledged. "I've also been having fun with it on frivolous ones," he added, so here we are. Russinovich noted that this was not Paint's first appearance in the world of "Can it run Doom?" However, earlier efforts rendered the game in a separate display and mirrored it into Paint. His version sends every frame through the Windows clipboard as a Device Independent Bitmap (DIB) and onto the canvas. Vibe-coding and the "Can it run Doom?" challenge were bound to meet. In 2025, Claude assisted an effort to use KiCad PCB design software to render Doom in vectors . Now Russinovich has enlisted it to turn Paint into a display. Azure may present its CTO with more pressing matters, but few will be as gloriously silly. ®

teaser: Experiencing a crisis? Get immediate help by texting HOME to 741-741 or calling/texting 988. Support is available 24/7.
summary: This article serves as a critical public service announcement, providing multiple resources for individuals experiencing emotional distress or crisis. Readers are advised that help is available at any time and location. Key services listed include the Crisis Text Line (Text HOME to 741-741) and the national lifeline, dialing or texting 988. Additional support is provided through The Trevor Project (texting START to 678-678) and international resources via the International Association for Suicide Prevention.
author: Emma Roth
content: If you or someone you know is considering suicide or is anxious, depressed, upset, or needs to talk, there are people who want to help. Crisis Text Line : Text HOME to 741-741 from anywhere in the US, at any time, about any type of crisis. 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline : Call or text 988 (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline). The original phone number, 1-800-273-TALK (8255), is available as well. The Trevor Project : Text START to 678-678 or call 1-866-488-7386 at any time to speak to a trained counselor. The International Association for Suicide Prevention lists a number of suicide hotlines by country. Click here to find them .
